sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Block storage is a low-level storage service that exposes fixed-size raw disk blocks to a compute instance over a network fabric (iSCSI, NVMe-oF, or vendor fabrics), which the guest OS formats with a filesystem and mounts like a local disk — delivering the lowest-latency, highest-IOPS storage in the cloud, suitable for databases and boot volumes.

Block storage is the storage layer that pretends to be a physical disk. When you launch an EC2 instance with an EBS volume, the OS sees `/dev/xvdf` and treats it exactly like a SATA drive attached to the motherboard: it runs `mkfs.ext4`, mounts it at `/data`, and every `read()` and `write()` syscall issues a block-level I/O. The catch is that the "disk" is actually a network-attached appliance — your instance and the EBS volume live in the same Availability Zone, and reads/writes traverse a dedicated storage network rather than a backplane bus. Modern NVMe-oF fabrics have narrowed this gap to sub-millisecond overhead, but the architecture is fundamentally "remote disk pretending to be local." AWS EBS, Azure Disk Storage, and Google Cloud Persistent Disk all follow this model, and they are the default storage for any workload that needs random reads and writes at single-digit-millisecond latency — which is to say, every relational database, every VM boot disk, and every message broker with persistent state.

The architecture of a block storage system is a cluster of storage nodes, each with many locally-attached NVMe SSDs, fronted by a controller that presents a virtual "volume" to the compute node. A volume is a logical abstraction: it has a size (e.g., 1TB), an IOPS limit (e.g., 16,000), and a throughput cap (e.g., 1,000 MB/s), and the controller maps its logical block addresses (LBAs) to physical disk offsets across the storage node's drives. Writes are acknowledged either after they hit the local SSD's write cache (write-back, fast but volatile) or after they are flushed to persistent media (write-through, slower but durable) — cloud providers default to write-through with synchronous replication to a standby replica in a second rack, so a single storage-node failure does not lose data. EBS, for example, replicates every write synchronously to two storage nodes in the same AZ within ~1ms, so the data is durable across a single-node failure but not across an AZ outage (for that you need EBS snapshots to S3, which are asynchronous). The IOPS and throughput caps are enforced at the controller via token-bucket rate limiting, which is why a gp3 volume can be "tuned" by paying more for higher IOPS — you are buying a bigger token bucket.

The defining trade-off of block storage is performance-over-shareability. A volume is attached to exactly one instance at a time (with limited multi-attach exceptions like EBS Multi-Attach, which is constrained to specific volume types and cluster quorum use cases). This means block storage is not a shared filesystem — two instances cannot both read and write the same volume concurrently without corrupting the filesystem, because the filesystem was not designed for concurrent writers. If you need shared access, you use file storage (NFS, SMB) or object storage instead. The performance benefit of this constraint is enormous: because the volume is single-writer, the controller does not need to coordinate locks across clients, and every I/O is a direct round-trip between the instance and the storage node — typically 0.5–2ms for SSD-backed volumes, with up to 256,000 IOPS and 4,000 MB/s throughput on the top io2 Block Express tier. For comparison, S3's first-byte latency is 20–50ms, and NFS over a network adds 1–5ms of protocol overhead on top of the underlying storage.

The real-world example is any database running in the cloud. When you deploy PostgreSQL on AWS, the data directory lives on an EBS io2 volume — the io2 tier is designed for databases because it offers sub-millisecond latency, 99.999% durability (versus 99.9% for gp3), and IOPS proportional to provisioned capacity. The PostgreSQL WAL (Write-Ahead Log) is the most latency-sensitive file in the system: every transaction commit must fsync the WAL, and a slow disk turns a 1ms commit into a 50ms commit, killing throughput. EBS io2 delivers the necessary latency and also supports snapshots — point-in-time, crash-consistent copies of the volume that are stored in S3 and can restore a new volume in minutes. When a DBA says "take a snapshot before the migration," the snapshot is a block-level copy: the EBS controller briefly flushes pending writes, takes a COW (copy-on-write) snapshot, and from that point forward every changed block on the original volume is also written to the snapshot store in S3. Restoring a snapshot creates a new volume and lazily fetches blocks from S3 as they are read — the first few minutes of reads are slow (blocks coming from S3), then the volume "warms up" as the hot blocks are cached on the storage node.

The cost model favors careful sizing. EBS gp3 is ~$0.08/GB-month for storage plus ~$0.005/provisioned-IOPS-month — a 1TB volume with 16,000 IOPS costs about $160/month, of which $80 is the IOPS. Over-provisioning IOPS is the most common waste; many workloads need 3,000 IOPS peak but are provisioned at 16,000 "just in case," doubling the cost. The architectural lesson is to measure first: use CloudWatch's `VolumeConsumedReadWriteOps` metric to size IOPS to actual peak, and use the gp3 tier (which decouples IOPS from capacity) rather than the older gp2 tier (which ties IOPS to size at 3 IOPS/GB). For databases that need higher durability, use io2 Block Express at ~$0.125/GB-month — the 99.999% durability justifies the 50% premium for irreplaceable data. Block storage is the right default for any workload with random I/O; it is the wrong choice for archival, large immutable objects, or anything that needs shared multi-client access.

sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart LR EC2[EC2 Instance
dev/xvdf] -->|NVMe-oF / iSCSI| Ctrl[Storage Controller
volume + IOPS policy] Ctrl --> Rep1[Storage Node 1
NVMe SSDs] Ctrl -.->|sync replica| Rep2[Storage Node 2
NVMe SSDs] Rep1 -.->|async snapshot| S3[(S3 Snapshot Store)] Ctrl -->|enforce IOPS / BW| TB[Token Bucket
rate limiter] Snap[Snap Restore] -->|lazy fetch| S3 Snap --> Ctrl ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-------------------+ | EC2 instance | | dev/xvdf (1 TB) | -> mkfs.ext4 -> mount /data +-------------------+ | | NVMe-oF fabric (sub-ms RTT, single AZ) v +-------------------+ sync replica (<1ms) | Storage Controller|------> +-------------------+ | LBA -> disk map | | Storage Node 2 | | token bucket | | replica of blocks| +-------------------+ +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Storage Node 1 | | NVMe SSD pool | | block 0..N | +-------------------+ | | async (background) v +-------------------+ | S3 snapshot store | (crash-consistent, COW) +-------------------+ ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The guest OS issues a `write()` syscall on a file; the local filesystem translates it into one or more block writes at specific LBAs on `/dev/xvdf`. 2. The block driver sends each write over NVMe-oF to the storage controller, which looks up the LBA-to-disk mapping, writes to the local NVMe SSD, and synchronously replicates to the standby storage node for durability; only after both acknowledgements does the controller return I/O completion. 3. A snapshot triggers a brief flush, after which changed blocks on the live volume are also written to S3 in the background; restoring a snapshot creates a new volume whose blocks are lazily fetched from S3 on first read.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
"""
Mini block storage mock: volumes of N blocks, raw block read/write,
synchronous replication to a standby, and crash-consistent snapshots.
"""
import time, hashlib
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

BLOCK_SIZE = 4096  # 4 KiB blocks, like a typical filesystem page

@dataclass
class Volume:
    name: str
    size_blocks: int
    blocks: list[bytes] = field(default_factory=list)
    iops_limit: int = 16000
    _ops_this_sec: int = 0
    _sec_start: float = 0.0

    def __post_init__(self):
        self.blocks = [b"\x00" * BLOCK_SIZE for _ in range(self.size_blocks)]

    def _rate_limit(self):
        now = time.time()
        if now - self._sec_start >= 1.0:
            self._sec_start, self._ops_this_sec = now, 0
        if self._ops_this_sec >= self.iops_limit:
            time.sleep(1.0 - (now - self._sec_start))
            self._sec_start, self._ops_this_sec = time.time(), 0
        self._ops_this_sec += 1

    def write_block(self, lba: int, payload: bytes):
        assert 0 <= lba < self.size_blocks, "LBA out of range"
        assert len(payload) <= BLOCK_SIZE, "payload exceeds block size"
        self._rate_limit()
        buf = payload + b"\x00" * (BLOCK_SIZE - len(payload))
        self.blocks[lba] = buf
        return True

    def read_block(self, lba: int) -> bytes:
        assert 0 <= lba < self.size_blocks, "LBA out of range"
        self._rate_limit()
        return self.blocks[lba]

    def flush_snapshot(self) -> str:
        # Crash-consistent: hash every block to fingerprint the state.
        h = hashlib.sha256()
        for b in self.blocks:
            h.update(b)
        return h.hexdigest()

class BlockStore:
    def __init__(self):
        self._volumes: dict[str, Volume] = {}
        self._replica: dict[str, Volume] = {}     # standby per volume
        self._snapshots: dict[str, list[bytes]] = {}  # S3-like snapshot store

    def create(self, name: str, size_gb: int, iops: int = 16000) -> Volume:
        n_blocks = (size_gb * 1024**3) // BLOCK_SIZE
        vol = Volume(name, n_blocks, iops_limit=iops)
        self._volumes[name] = vol
        self._replica[name] = Volume(name + "_repl", n_blocks, iops_limit=iops)
        return vol

    def write(self, name: str, lba: int, payload: bytes):
        vol = self._volumes[name]
        vol.write_block(lba, payload)               # primary write
        self._replica[name].blocks[lba] = vol.blocks[lba]  # sync replica

    def read(self, name: str, lba: int) -> bytes:
        return self._volumes[name].read_block(lba)

    def snapshot(self, name: str) -> str:
        snap_id = f"snap-{int(time.time())}-{name}"
        self._snapshots[snap_id] = list(self._volumes[name].blocks)  # COW base
        return snap_id

    def restore(self, snap_id: str, new_name: str) -> Volume:
        blocks = self._snapshots[snap_id]
        vol = Volume(new_name, len(blocks))
        vol.blocks = list(blocks)  # lazy fetch in real life; here we copy
        self._volumes[new_name] = vol
        return vol

if __name__ == "__main__":
    bs = BlockStore()
    bs.create("pg_data", size_gb=1, iops=3000)   # 1 GiB volume, 3000 IOPS
    payload = b"INSERT INTO orders ..." + b"\x00" * 100
    bs.write("pg_data", lba=42, payload=payload)
    print("Read back:", bs.read("pg_data", 42)[:25])
    snap = bs.snapshot("pg_data")
    bs.write("pg_data", lba=42, payload=b"OVERWRITTEN")   # post-snap write
    print("Live block:", bs.read("pg_data", 42)[:11])
    restored = bs.restore(snap, "pg_data_restored")
    print("Restored block:", restored.read_block(42)[:25])  # original content
```

quiz.explanation: Ephemeral block storage is local to the host running the instance — it is the NVMe SSDs physically inside the server — and its lifetime is tied to the instance: stop or terminate the instance and the data is gone. Persistent block storage (EBS, Azure Disk, GCP Persistent Disk) is network-attached and lives independently of the instance, so you can stop, restart, or migrate the instance without losing data.

quiz.explanation: EBS durability comes from synchronous replication: every write to a volume is acknowledged only after it has been persisted to two storage nodes in different racks within the same AZ. This protects against single-node failure (the standby has the data), single-rack power loss (the replica is in a different rack), and individual SSD failures (the storage node's own RAID rebuilds transparently).

Throughput is bytes per second — IOPS × block size, capped at the volume's throughput limit. Latency is the time from issuing an I/O to its completion, dominated by the storage medium (NVMe ~0.1ms, network overhead ~0.5–2ms in EBS).

quiz.explanation: EBS snapshots are point-in-time, block-level copies stored in S3. The mechanism is copy-on-write: when you trigger a snapshot, EBS briefly pauses writes, records the current state of every block's metadata, and resumes I/O; from that point forward, every block that is overwritten on the live volume is first copied to the snapshot store in S3.
